rv.q: Yet, despite dramatic shortcomings, this is a startling, angry production that may sharpen theatre’s cutlass.
Malkovich deserved a more rounded and thought-provoking play.
Its first half is broadly what you might expect, and kind of okay if you’re willing to overlook the relentlessly male viewpoint and total lack of subtlety.
The upshot is a thin comedy that is upsetting for the wrong reasons.

David Mamet’s new play is billed as a dark farce and an attempt to examine the #MeToo movement from an unfamiliar angle. But instead of prompting nuanced discussion, it has the rancid smell of clickbait.
Bitter Wheat fails on every front.
I could have watched this captivating freak-show until midnight and beyond.
A passable performance from Malkovich cannot save this play, or make it into something it's not.
As directed by Mamet himself, the entire play lands on stage like an ugly lump of exactly the commodity Fein is so proud of selling to an unsuspecting public.
Implausible, daft and irritating, Bitter Wheat leaves a very bad taste.
"Bitter Wheat" is as flaccid as a deflated balloon: a half-assed amalgamation of an attempted sexual assault, regurgitated from reports and rumors, served up as a sloppy, second-rate farce.
